It is no use, young man, you can’t open it! How he does call and pound! Now he’s crying for an axe. It would be a shame to break down that beautiful door! “John dear!” said I in the gentlest voice, “the key is down by the front steps, under a plantain leaf!” That silenced him for a few moments. Then he said—very quietly indeed, “Open the door, my darling!” “I can’t,” said I. “The key is down by the front door, under a plantain leaf!” And then I said it again, several times, very gently and slowly, and said it so often that he had to go and see, and he got it, of course, and came in. He stopped short by the door. “What is the matter?” he cried. “For God’s sake, what are you doing?” I kept on creeping just the same, but I looked at him over my shoulder. “I’ve got out at last,” said I, “in spite of you and Jane! And I’ve pulled off most of the paper, so you can’t put me back!” Now why should that man have fainted? But he did, and right across my path by the wall, so that I had to creep over him every time! ABOUT THE AUTHOR Born in Hartford, Connecticut, Charlotte Perkins Gilman (1860–1935) was an A merican novelist, short story writer, poet, editor, lecturer, commercial artist, and utopian feminist. Though her schooling was limited and erratic—leaving her largely self-taught—she amassed a breadth of knowledge, pursuing intellectual studies, artistic endeavors, and feminist advocacy. She would go on to become an organizer of social reform and a prominent lecturer noted for her unorthodox concepts of marriage, women’s suffrage, humanism, and patriarchal subjugation. Gilman was the author of several poetry collections, novels and novellas, and nearly two hundred short stories, including The Yellow Wallpaper , which was inspired by a severe bout of postpartum depression. In 1994, she was inducted into the National Women’s Hall of Fame.
